description: Macronutrients, micronutrients, energy balance and how dehydration affects sport performance.
content_html:
Why Nutrition Matters in Sport

Food is the body’s fuel. The amount, type and timing of what an athlete eats directly affects how much energy they have during training, how quickly they recover afterwards, whether their body composition supports their sport and how strongly their immune and skeletal systems resist injury and illness. A thorough understanding of nutrition is therefore not a separate subject from PE — it is integral to physical performance.

Macronutrients

Macronutrients are the energy-providing nutrients. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A balanced diet for an active individual should provide approximately 55–60% of energy from carbohydrates, 25–30% from fats and 15–20% from proteins.

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred and most readily available energy source. They are broken down to glucose, which is used directly for energy production or stored as glycogen in the liver and skeletal muscles. Glycogen is the key fuel for moderate-to-high-intensity exercise. When glycogen stores are depleted, performance deteriorates rapidly — athletes call this “hitting the wall” in endurance events. Carbohydrate loading is a strategy used by endurance athletes such as marathon runners, who increase carbohydrate intake in the days before a race to maximise glycogen stores. A runner preparing for a marathon might shift from a standard 55% carbohydrate diet to 70% in the final 48 hours before the race.

Proteins are made up of amino acids and are essential for the growth, repair and maintenance of body tissues, particularly muscle. During resistance training, microscopic tears occur in muscle fibres. Protein consumed after training provides the amino acids needed to repair these tears and build new, stronger muscle tissue — a process called hypertrophy. The timing of protein intake matters: consuming protein within 30–60 minutes after a resistance session maximises the muscle-repair response. For power athletes such as weightlifters or sprinters, protein intake is especially important because muscle mass is central to their performance.

Fats are a concentrated energy source providing more than twice the energy per gram as carbohydrates or proteins. They are the primary fuel for low-intensity, prolonged exercise — long, easy-paced cycling or walking. The body stores fat in virtually unlimited quantities and draws on it during aerobic activity when glycogen stores begin to deplete. Fats are also essential for the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), the production of hormones and the maintenance of cell membranes. Unsaturated fats from sources such as olive oil, nuts and oily fish are health-promoting, whereas excessive saturated fat (from red meat and full-fat dairy) raises LDL cholesterol and increases cardiovascular disease risk.

Key Fact

Balanced diet macronutrient split: carbohydrates 55–60% (primary fuel, stored as glycogen), fats 25–30% (secondary fuel, hormone production), proteins 15–20% (tissue repair and hypertrophy). Endurance athletes increase carbohydrate proportion before major events; power athletes prioritise protein timing after resistance training.

Micronutrients

Micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — do not provide energy but are essential for many critical processes. Iron is needed to form haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells; a deficiency causes anaemia, reducing aerobic capacity. Calcium is the primary mineral in bone structure; adequate calcium intake throughout adolescence maximises bone density, reducing lifelong fracture risk. Vitamin D enables calcium absorption from the gut and is therefore equally important for bone health. Athletes who train indoors or in low-sunlight climates may develop vitamin D deficiency, increasing their risk of stress fractures. Water and fibre, while not traditional micronutrients, are also essential: fibre supports healthy digestion and water enables every cellular process in the body.

Many students believe that eating large amounts of protein will automatically cause muscle bulk. In reality, dietary protein alone does not cause hypertrophy — it must be combined with progressive resistance training. Protein provides the raw material (amino acids) for muscle repair; the training stimulus provides the reason to repair bigger. An endurance athlete who increases protein intake without changing their training will simply excrete the excess as urea rather than building new muscle. This is an important nuance for 4-mark explain questions about nutrition and performance.

Energy Balance

Energy balance is the relationship between energy consumed (through food and drink) and energy expended (through basal metabolic rate and physical activity). When intake equals expenditure, weight is stable. When intake exceeds expenditure, the surplus is stored as fat and weight increases. When expenditure exceeds intake, the body draws on fat stores and weight decreases. Maintaining an appropriate energy balance is essential for athletes: too little energy causes fatigue, muscle loss and hormonal disruption; too much causes unwanted fat gain and reduced power-to-weight ratio. The correct balance varies between sports: an ultra-endurance athlete needs a very high caloric intake, while a gymnast needs carefully controlled intake to maintain the strength-to-weight ratio that their sport demands.

Hydration and Dehydration

Water makes up around 60% of adult body mass and is involved in every physiological process relevant to exercise: transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood, regulating body temperature through sweating, lubricating joints and removing waste products via urine. Even mild dehydration — a loss of just 2% of body water — measurably impairs aerobic performance and decision-making ability. As dehydration worsens, blood volume decreases, which makes the blood thicker. This raises blood viscosity, forcing the heart to work harder to deliver the same amount of oxygen to the muscles. Heart rate rises, perceived effort increases and endurance performance deteriorates.

At higher levels of dehydration (above 5% body water loss), the risk of heat exhaustion and heat stroke increases significantly. Cramping, dizziness and collapse become possible during prolonged exercise in warm conditions. Athletes should begin exercise well hydrated (pale yellow urine is a common guide) and drink regularly throughout prolonged activity rather than waiting until they feel thirsty — thirst is already a late signal of dehydration. Sports drinks that contain electrolytes (sodium and potassium) as well as carbohydrates are useful in events lasting more than 60 minutes, as they replace both fluid and the electrolytes lost in sweat.

Key Fact

Dehydration chain: blood volume decreases → blood viscosity increases → heart works harder to maintain cardiac output → heart rate rises → fatigue increases and endurance performance deteriorates. Even 2% dehydration measurably impairs aerobic performance.

Carbohydrate loading works by maximising glycogen storage in the muscles and liver before a prolonged endurance event. Athletes typically taper their training (reducing volume while maintaining intensity) and simultaneously increase carbohydrate intake in the 48–72 hours before competition. The strategy is effective for events lasting more than 90 minutes (such as a marathon or triathlon) because it delays the point at which glycogen depletion causes fatigue. It is not appropriate for short, high-intensity events (such as the 100m sprint) where glycogen stores are not the limiting factor. A sprinter does not benefit from carbohydrate loading in the same way because their event is over in under 15 seconds and relies primarily on the ATP-PC (phosphocreatine) energy system.
exam_tip_html: For questions about macronutrients, always name the specific function of each one, not just “they provide energy.” Carbohydrates for fuel and glycogen storage; protein for muscle repair and hypertrophy; fats for low-intensity fuel and hormone production — these distinctions earn the marks. For dehydration questions, describe the physiological chain of events (blood volume → viscosity → heart rate) rather than simply saying “you get tired.” A common mistake on calculate questions involving energy balance or macronutrient percentages is to forget to show the calculation — always write the formula, substitute the values and state the unit in your answer.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Macronutrient split for an active person: 55–60% carbohydrates (primary fuel, glycogen), 25–30% fats (secondary fuel, hormones), 15–20% protein (repair and hypertrophy). Timing matters: protein within 60 minutes post-resistance training maximises adaptation.
  • Micronutrients such as iron (haemoglobin, aerobic capacity) and calcium (bone density) are essential for performance. Deficiency in either can directly impair training outcomes or increase injury risk.
  • Dehydration reduces blood volume, increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate and reduces endurance performance — even 2% water loss is measurable. Athletes should maintain hydration before, during and after exercise.

practice_questions.text: A distance runner consumes 3,000 kcal per day. If 57% of this comes from carbohydrates and each gram of carbohydrate provides 4 kcal, calculate how many grams of carbohydrate she consumes daily.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: 3,000 kcal x 0.57 = 1,710 kcal from carbohydrates; 1 mark for correct final answer with units: 1,710 ÷ 4 = 427.5 g of carbohydrate.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'hypertrophy' and explain why protein timing is important for power athletes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining hypertrophy: an increase in muscle fibre size resulting from resistance training. 1 mark for stating that protein provides the amino acids needed for muscle repair and growth after training. 1 mark for explaining the timing importance: consuming protein within 30-60 minutes after training maximises the muscle-repair response when fibres are most receptive to amino acid uptake.

practice_questions.text: Explain why even mild dehydration reduces an athlete's endurance performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that dehydration reduces blood volume; 1 mark for explaining that reduced blood volume increases blood viscosity, making blood thicker and harder to pump; 1 mark for linking this to the effect on performance (the heart must beat faster to maintain cardiac output, increasing perceived effort and causing earlier fatigue).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows the macronutrient intake of two athletes: Athlete A (sprinter) takes in 18% carbohydrate, 47% fat, 35% protein. Athlete B (marathon runner) takes in 65% carbohydrate, 20% fat, 15% protein. Interpret what this data suggests about how well each athlete's diet matches their sport's demands.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly reading/comparing the data (Athlete A is low in carbohydrate and very high in protein and fat; Athlete B has a high carbohydrate intake); 1 mark for assessing Athlete B's diet as appropriate (marathon running requires sustained aerobic effort fuelled by glycogen; 65% carbohydrate supports glycogen stores and delays fatigue); 1 mark for assessing Athlete A's diet as potentially problematic (sprinters also benefit from adequate carbohydrate for explosive anaerobic energy; 18% is below recommended levels and the very high fat intake is not optimal); 1 mark for a comparative evaluative statement (Athlete B's diet is better matched to sport demands; Athlete A may need to increase carbohydrate intake to optimise performance).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level hockey player wants to improve her body composition and sporting performance through dietary changes. Analyse the role of macronutrients in achieving her goals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three macronutrients discussed with accurate roles and sport-specific application to hockey; timing of protein mentioned; carbohydrate loading not applicable here but appropriate carbohydrate fuelling for training discussed; energy balance considered; technically accurate language.

Secure: At least two macronutrients discussed with mostly accurate roles; hockey application present; some mention of quantity or timing.

Developing: One or two macronutrients described; limited sport application; limited analysis of how dietary changes achieve the specific goals stated.

Emerging: Basic statement that diet affects performance with little specific macronutrient detail.

Acceptable content: carbohydrates — primary fuel for the high-intensity sprinting and repeated efforts in hockey; adequate glycogen stores prevent mid-game fatigue; proteins — hockey involves physical contact and repeated muscle loading; post-training protein (within 60 min) promotes muscle repair and lean mass gain, improving body composition; fats — provide energy during lighter training days; essential for hormone production; unsaturated fats from healthy sources preferred; energy balance — she needs to expend slightly more than she consumes to lose fat while maintaining lean mass, avoiding too large a deficit which would impair recovery.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of carbohydrate loading for endurance athletes, considering both the evidence in favour and possible limitations of the strategy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of carbohydrate loading including the physiological rationale, the type of athlete it benefits, the specific protocol and the evidence of effectiveness; limitations discussed (not suitable for short events, can cause GI discomfort, requires tapering); balanced conclusion with a justified judgement.

Secure: Both benefits and limitations present; endurance context well developed; some physiological detail; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly benefits described with limited limitations; some physiological explanation; argument mainly descriptive.

Emerging: Basic description of carbohydrate loading with little evaluation.

In favour: maximises muscle and liver glycogen stores; delays the point of glycogen depletion ('hitting the wall') in events over 90 minutes; allows the athlete to maintain race pace for longer; particularly effective for marathon runners, cyclists and triathletes who perform for 2+ hours.

Limitations: not appropriate for events under 90 minutes (glycogen depletion is not the limiting factor); sprinters, team-sport players and gymnasts do not benefit significantly; some athletes experience gastrointestinal discomfort with very high carbohydrate intake; the strategy requires careful planning and coordination with taper; extra glycogen storage is accompanied by water retention (glycogen binds water), which can feel heavy and is a concern for weight-class or aesthetic sports.

Conclusion: carbohydrate loading is highly effective and evidence-based for the right athlete in the right event, but it is not a universal strategy and must be matched to the specific demands of the sport.

knowledge_checks.q: Which macronutrient is the body's preferred fuel source during moderate-to-high-intensity exercise?
A loss of what percentage of body water is sufficient to measurably impair aerobic performance?
Dehydration increases blood _____, making it harder for the heart to pump blood around the body.
Protein consumed after resistance training provides the amino acids needed for muscle repair and _____.
Match each macronutrient to its primary role:
right: Stored as glycogen, primary exercise fuel

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of a balanced diet should come from carbohydrates?
What is carbohydrate stored as in the muscles and liver?
Why is protein timing important for power athletes after training?
flashcard_questions.a: Consuming protein within 60 minutes maximises muscle repair and hypertrophy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hypertrophy and what causes it in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: An increase in muscle fibre size, caused by resistance training and adequate protein intake.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of fat is associated with heart-healthy effects?
What is blood viscosity and why does it matter in dehydration?
flashcard_questions.a: The thickness of blood; dehydration increases it, forcing the heart to work harder.

flashcard_questions.q: Which mineral is needed to form haemoglobin for oxygen transport?
Which micronutrient enables calcium absorption and supports bone health?

flashcard_questions.a: The relationship between energy consumed in food and energy expended through activity.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of athlete benefits most from carbohydrate loading?
flashcard_questions.a: Endurance athletes in events lasting over 90 minutes, such as marathon runners.

flashcard_questions.q: Which macronutrient is the body's primary fuel source during moderate-to-high-intensity exercise?
What signs indicate an athlete is starting to dehydrate during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Raised heart rate and increased perceived effort for the same workload.

glossary_terms.definition: Nutrients required in large amounts that provide the body with energy and the building blocks for growth and repair: carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
The body's primary and most efficient fuel source, broken down to glucose for immediate energy or stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
An increase in the size of muscle fibres resulting from resistance training and adequate protein intake.
Fats that are liquid at room temperature and come mostly from plant sources; associated with heart-healthy effects.
Vitamins and minerals required in small amounts that support essential body processes without directly providing energy.
The relationship between energy consumed in food and energy expended through metabolism and physical activity.
The resistance of blood to flowing smoothly through vessels; it increases with dehydration, forcing the heart to work harder.
